cards.front: What federal law created the SEC, and what is the SEC's primary role?
cards.back: The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 created the SEC. It is the securities industry's primary regulatory body, with authority over broker-dealers, exchanges, trading markets, securities information providers, and (via delegation to FINRA) the licensing of securities representatives.

cards.front: List the sanctions the SEC may impose on a broker-dealer that fails to comply with its rules.
cards.back: Censure; limits on activities, functions, or operations; suspension of registration (firm or associated person); revocation of registration (including permanent bar); and/or fines. Note: the SEC cannot arrest violators — that requires law enforcement.

cards.front: May a broker-dealer state in its advertising that it is 'SEC-approved' because it is registered with the SEC?
cards.back: No. Registration with the SEC does not imply that the SEC has passed upon or approved the BD's financial standing, business, or conduct. Any such claim is misrepresentation.

cards.front: Beyond creating the SEC, what other areas does the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 regulate?
cards.back: Secondary market trading; insider transactions, short sales, and proxies; customer accounts; the customer protection rule; net capital and financial responsibility for BDs; and issuer reporting requirements (e.g., annual reports).

cards.front: Security (for SIE purposes)
cards.back: An intangible financial asset that may be bought, sold, or gifted between persons, represented by a paper certificate or electronic record. Commodities (gold, oil, beef) and futures on them are NOT securities.

cards.front: FinCEN (Financial Crimes Enforcement Network)
cards.back: A bureau of the U.S. Treasury that safeguards the financial system from illicit use, combats money laundering, and promotes national security through collection and analysis of financial intelligence. Financial firms file suspicious activity and large cash transaction reports with FinCEN.

cards.front: What is the role of the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) in financial regulation?
cards.back: It supervises national banks, federal savings associations, and U.S. branches/agencies of foreign banks, ensuring they operate safely, treat customers fairly, and comply with law. The Comptroller also serves as a director of the FDIC.

cards.front: On the SIE, what is the critical distinction between 'OCC' and 'Office of the Comptroller of the Currency'?
cards.back: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency is a Treasury bureau that regulates national banks. The abbreviation 'OCC' refers to the Options Clearing Corporation, an SRO for the options market. They are unrelated.

cards.front: What role does the IRS play with respect to broker-dealers?
cards.back: The IRS is the federal tax enforcement agency. BDs and most financial services firms must provide customer and firm information to the IRS on demand. The IRS enforces, but does not write, tax law.

cards.front: What are the SIPC coverage limits?
cards.back: Up to $500,000 per separate customer (separate capacity), of which no more than $250,000 may be cash. Securities are valued at market; in margin accounts, only equity is covered.

cards.front: Which broker-dealers registered with the SEC are NOT required to be SIPC members?
cards.back: Banks dealing exclusively in municipal securities; firms dealing exclusively in U.S. government securities; and firms dealing exclusively in redeemable investment company (mutual fund) securities.

cards.front: John Doe has a cash account and a margin account at the same BD. Are these accounts covered separately by SIPC?
cards.back: No. Cash and margin accounts of the same customer are combined and treated as a single separate-capacity account, covered up to $500,000 (no more than $250,000 cash). Only the equity in the margin account is covered.

cards.front: Maria has three accounts at one BD: an individual account, a joint account with her spouse, and an IRA. How does SIPC treat them?
cards.back: Each is a separate capacity, so each is covered up to $500,000 (max $250,000 cash) — three separate $500,000 limits.

cards.front: What happens to a customer whose claims exceed SIPC coverage limits when a BD fails?
cards.back: The customer becomes a general creditor of the failed BD for the uncovered amount.

cards.front: Are commodities, futures contracts, and currency positions covered by SIPC?
cards.back: No. Commodities, commodities futures, and currency contracts/losses are not securities and are not covered by SIPC.

cards.front: What disclosure requirements apply to SIPC membership advertising?
cards.back: BDs must display SIPC membership in advertising and post a sign at the firm. The term 'SIPC' may not appear larger than the firm's own name. Written SIPC disclosure (including how to obtain the SIPC brochure) must be given at account opening and at least annually thereafter. Firms may not imply their SIPC coverage is greater or unique.

cards.front: What are the FDIC coverage limits, and what types of accounts are covered?
cards.back: $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. Covers checking, savings, money market deposit accounts, CDs, and self-directed IRA deposits. Does NOT cover mutual funds, annuities, life insurance, stocks, or bonds.

cards.front: Gabriel has $200,000 in an individual account, and Gabriel and Lisa jointly hold $450,000 at the same FDIC-insured bank. If the bank fails, what is covered?
cards.back: Gabriel's $200,000 individual account is covered in full (under $250,000). The joint account is covered up to $250,000 per owner — Gabriel $225,000 + Lisa $225,000 = the full $450,000 is covered.

cards.front: How does SIPC coverage differ structurally from FDIC coverage?
cards.back: SIPC: $500,000 per separate-capacity account (not per owner on the account). FDIC: $250,000 per depositor (owner) per ownership category. A joint FDIC account is covered per owner; a joint SIPC account is one separate capacity covered up to $500,000 total.

cards.front: Uniform Securities Act (USA)
cards.back: A 1956 federal template for state securities laws, adopted by all states (with minor variations). It requires each state to have a securities administrator with authority over the registration of securities, BDs, IAs, and representatives.

cards.front: State securities administrator
cards.back: The official in each state with authority over the registration of securities, broker-dealers, investment advisers, and representatives within that state. May be appointed or elected; title varies by state.

cards.front: NASAA (North American Securities Administrators Association)
cards.back: The association of state and provincial securities regulators in the U.S., Canada, and Mexico. Has no direct regulatory authority but issues Model Rules that administrators use in enforcing state law.

cards.front: To register a broker-dealer firm to do business in a particular state, with whom do you register?
cards.back: The state securities administrator of that state. (NASAA is an association, not a registration authority.)

cards.front: Match each Act to its purpose: Securities Act of 1933; Securities Exchange Act of 1934; Investment Company Act of 1940; Investment Advisers Act of 1940; SIPA 1970; Insider Trading Act of 1988; USA PATRIOT Act 2001.
cards.back: 1933 — primary market/new issues registration; 1934 — secondary market, BD/exchange regulation, SEC created; ICA 1940 — packaged products (mutual funds, CEFs, UITs); IAA 1940 — investment advisers; SIPA 1970 — customer protection in BD bankruptcy (created SIPC); 1988 — insider trading penalties; PATRIOT Act 2001 — AML policies and procedures.
